Trials now report what they cost.

The workspace agent's token usage and USD cost land in harbor's own fields (`n_input_tokens`, `n_cache_tokens`, `n_output_tokens`, `cost_usd` on the trial result, plus `final_metrics` on the trajectory), so `harbor view` and any job-level aggregation pick them up without bespoke readers. The numbers come from the per-message `usage` blocks already present in the workspace event stream, so nothing extra is collected from the workspace and a timed-out trial still accounts for what it spent.

A new `agent/usage.json` artifact carries the full breakdown: uncached input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens kept as separate non-overlapping buckets, per model, with per-model costs. Anthropic prices those three input classes differently (a cache write costs 1.25x a plain input token, a cache read 0.1x), so collapsing them cannot produce a correct cost and hides cache behaviour. Prices come from `mngr_usage`'s table rather than a local copy, which keeps them bound to what the LiteLLM proxy bills; a model missing from that table reports a null cost rather than a misleading zero, and a trial whose transcript carries no usage at all reports null rather than zero.

The decider (the simulated user) is now reported separately under `metadata.decider_usage`, with its own token counts and cost. It previously occupied the trial's `n_input_tokens` / `n_output_tokens` fields, which read as though the agent under test had consumed them.

Trials that delegate are flagged rather than silently undercounted. The workspace events endpoint serves main-session events only -- a subagent's turns go to a separate per-subagent stream, and work handed to a newly created worker agent lives on that agent's stream -- so neither reaches the totals. Left unmarked, an agent that delegates would report a lower cost than one doing the same work inline, which makes the metric gameable. `is_cost_complete` now reports whether the total accounts for everything the agent caused, alongside an exact count of `Agent` tool calls and a heuristic count of worker launches.

Workspaces are now signed in the way a user signs in. The driver posts credentials to the workspace's own `/api/claude-auth/submit-credentials` after create, gated on `/api/claude-auth/status` answering, and waits for the chat agent to come back to WAITING (the endpoint restarts the claude agents). Previously the key was injected into the workspace host env at create time via `MINDS_EXTRA_PASS_HOST_ENV`, which forced `MNGR__AGENT_TYPES__CLAUDE__ISOLATE_LOCAL_CONFIG_DIR=true` to avoid deadlocking on Claude Code's unknown-key dialog. Both are gone: the box env now carries no AI credentials at all.

This matters beyond tidiness. A workspace boots unauthenticated because the product's create path supplies no AI credentials, and the workspace's auth module states credentials must never go in the mngr host env file, which is frozen into supervisord and its services at boot. The eval was reconstructing a route the product had deliberately removed, and paying for it by grading an agent provisioned down a different code path than real workspaces use. Signing in through the endpoint puts the graded agent back in production's shared config-dir regime, and gives the driver a real auth readiness gate where it previously had none. `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, when set, is submitted alongside the key, so the same path can point a workspace at a proxy.

The sign-in result is checked rather than assumed. The endpoint deliberately runs no credential probe -- a wrong key or base URL is accepted and surfaces only later, as the agent replying that it is not logged in, which the judge would then grade as the agent's own behaviour. The driver now requires the workspace to come back reporting `logged_in` and the auth mode matching what was submitted (`api_key` for a bare key, `imbue` when a base URL rides along).

Zero-token synthetic messages no longer void a trial's cost. Claude Code reports its pre-sign-in "Not logged in" notice as a `<synthetic>` model with an all-zero usage block; because that pseudo-model has no price, it was making otherwise fully priceable trials report an unknown cost.

Added an opt-in reverse-tunnel probe (`--ak proxy_probe=true`), groundwork for running an LLM proxy inside the eval box so every model call is metered at a boundary the graded agent cannot route around. A Modal sandbox cannot open a tunnel to itself at run time, so the only way into the box is the SSH channel mngr already holds open to the workspace, used in reverse -- the same mechanism minds uses in production to reach the desktop gateway. The probe serves a token on a box-local port, asks the workspace's sshd to forward back to it, and fetches the URL from inside the workspace to confirm the round trip. Off by default.

Added the configuration for an in-box LiteLLM proxy: a model list generated from `mngr_usage`'s price table (so the proxy's costs and the eval's transcript arithmetic cannot disagree about prices, and a model added there becomes routable without a second edit), plus the auth and usage hooks it loads. The proxy runs with no database -- LiteLLM's schema is Postgres-only and a fresh one costs about a hundred migrations, far too much per trial -- so virtual keys and spend tables are unavailable and both are supplied by the hooks instead: one per-trial key, and one JSON line per request with the cache buckets kept separate. That trade is what keeps Modal the only infrastructure this eval depends on.

Verified against the real Anthropic API rather than only in tests: a wrong key is refused, a valid one routes and is billed, prompt caching survives the proxy intact (a call through it read 4,402 cached tokens written by a direct call), and LiteLLM's own cost for a request reproduces exactly what `mngr_usage`'s table computes from the recorded buckets. The recorded token counts are normalized to non-overlapping buckets, because LiteLLM reports prompt tokens inclusive of cache while the eval's transcript accounting reports them exclusive -- mixing the two conventions would price cached tokens at the full input rate on top of the cache rate.

Corrected a significant overcount in the transcript accounting, found by metering the same trial two ways. One API response becomes several transcript messages -- one per content block -- and each carries a copy of the response's usage, so summing every message counted the same tokens two or three times. Consecutive messages reporting identical usage for the same model are collapsed into the one response they came from. On the trial where both sources ran, this brings the transcript from $3.55 to $1.8967 against the proxy's independently metered $1.8967, on 29 responses against the proxy's 29 requests. Every cost this app reported before this fix was inflated by roughly a factor of two.

The workspace can now be routed through the in-box proxy with `--ak proxy=true`. The driver starts LiteLLM in the box, reverse-tunnels it so the workspace reaches it as a loopback address, and signs the workspace in with that address and a freshly minted per-trial key -- never the upstream credential, so what the agent can read buys nothing outside its own trial. The proxy's per-request log lands in `agent/usage_proxy.jsonl`. Because the workspace's claude agents share one credential, subagents and worker agents route through it too, which is the delegated spend the transcript cannot see.

Verified that the proxy captures delegated spend, which is the reason it exists. Across the small dataset with `--ak proxy=true`: on the two cases that delegated nothing the proxy and the transcript agreed to the cent (35 responses/35 requests at $2.0989, and 27/27 at $1.5158), and on the case that launched a worker they diverged by exactly that worker's spend -- 44 responses and $2.8647 by transcript against 69 requests and $5.2330 through the proxy. Delegation is not deterministic, so the same case delegates on one run and not the next, which is why a metering boundary is worth more than a list of delegation routes. (Those dollar figures are standard-rate, measured before the fast-mode pricing below; the same trials would report about twice that now. The agreement and the divergence between the two sources are what the numbers are there to show, and neither depends on the rate.)

When a proxy ran, harbor's token and cost fields now come from it rather than from the transcript, since it is the complete account; the transcript's own figures are kept under `metadata.transcript_usage` so the two can still be reconciled per trial.

Fast mode is now visible in the accounting, and priced correctly. Minds runs its chat agent in fast mode by default, and fast mode bills the same tokens at twice the standard rate ($10/$50 per MTok against $5/$25 on Opus 5 and Opus 4.8). Nothing in the response reports a price, so every dollar figure in this system is arithmetic over a rate table, and every eval cost reported before this was computed at the standard rate -- roughly half of what a fast-mode trial actually cost, with nothing to indicate it.

The proxy now records the tier per request, and each tier's tokens are priced at that tier's rate, so a trial that ran in fast mode reports what it actually cost rather than half of it. The fast-mode portion is also reported as its own subset of the totals (`fast_message_count`, `fast_tokens`, per model as well as overall), so the split is visible rather than only folded into a dollar figure. A source that cannot see the tier -- the transcript -- prices everything standard and reports `is_cost_rate_certain: false`, marking that number as a floor rather than a measurement.

This is a second and separate axis from `is_cost_complete`: that one asks whether all the traffic is in the total, this one whether the traffic in it is priced at the rate it was billed at.

Only the proxy can see the tier. The workspace event stream carries token counts but no speed, so a transcript-sourced total always reports it as unknown -- one more thing `--ak proxy=true` buys. The tier is read from the request parameter LiteLLM actually sends upstream, not from `usage.speed` in the response: LiteLLM blanks that field when it normalizes the provider response, and the raw body it would otherwise be recoverable from is retained only for non-streaming calls, while real workspace traffic streams. Reading the request is sound because that value is taken after LiteLLM drops parameters the target model does not accept, and the API rejects an unsupported `speed` rather than quietly serving the request standard.

Worth knowing before comparing models: fast mode is Opus-only -- the API returns a 400 for `speed` on Sonnet and Haiku -- and switching tier invalidates the prompt cache. A per-model comparison that leaves fast mode at its default is therefore not comparing like with like, and would be attributing a rate difference to the model.

Verified against a real proxied trial: a live Minds workspace asked for fast mode on all 23 of its requests, confirming that the default really is on and that every eval cost recorded before this was half of what the trial cost. Repricing that trial by tier gives $2.955128 against the $1.477564 the standard rate produces -- exactly 2x, and the standard figure reproduces LiteLLM's own summed per-request cost to the digit, which is the expected relationship since a LiteLLM model entry carries one price.

That trial also exposed a real gap: the transcript trailed the proxy by two requests with no delegation involved, its 21 responses mapping one-for-one onto the proxy's first 21. The driver stopped reading the event stream the moment the agent reported WAITING, so anything the agent did afterwards -- the workspace's own turn-end flow runs then -- was never fetched, and destroying the workspace made it unrecoverable. The driver now pulls once more after WAITING and again before the transcript is written for the last time.

One known imprecision is now documented rather than fixed: every prompt-cache write is priced at the 5-minute-TTL rate (1.25x an input token), and Anthropic bills a 1-hour write at 2x. Nothing in the chain from the workspace to the cost figure carries the TTL, so a trial whose agent asks for the longer cache understates that bucket by 37.5%.
